transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess... I mean, I came in because things have just been feeling really off lately, you know? It's kind of hard to explain, but it’s been going on for the last few weeks. I work surveillance, mostly nights, and usually, when I get off shift, I’m starving. I'd swing by the diner or grab something on the way home, you know, maybe a burger or even just some leftover pizza. I used to really look forward to it. It was like my reward for staring at monitors for eight hours straight. But lately... I don't know, I just barely have an appetite at all. It’s like my stomach is just completely empty, but my brain doesn’t care. Even the foods I usually really like, the stuff I’d crave at 3 AM, I just... I look at it, and it just sits there. I try to eat because I know I need to, I know I need the energy to stay awake on the job, but I just end up forcing down a few bites and then I can't do it anymore. It's just too much effort. I don't know if it's the schedule catching up to me or what, but it's really starting to bother me because I'm just not eating like I used to.
Have you been feeling sad or down most of the time lately?

Yeah, I suppose you could say that. But it’s almost... I don't know if "sad" is exactly the right word, you know? It’s more like... well, most days I feel like I’m carrying this heavy, flat feeling around with me everywhere I go. I was actually trying to figure out how to explain it to my wife the other day, because it’s not like I’m sitting around crying or anything like that. It’s just this weight. 

And it doesn't really matter where I am or what I'm doing, it just follows me. Like, I’ll be sitting in the break room at work—we’ve got this little room right behind the main monitor banks with a coffee machine and a couple of those cheap plastic chairs—and the other guys will be in there joking around, talking about a game or whatever, and I just feel completely flat. I can't even force a laugh. 

Or even when I get off shift and I'm finally home. I’ll be sitting right there on the couch in the living room with my family, and they’re talking or watching a show, and physically I’m right there with them, but... I just feel like I’m not really there. It's like I'm a million miles away, or like there's this pane of glass between me and everyone else. I'm just sort of existing in the room. So yeah, I guess it is feeling down, but it's just so constant, this heavy flatness, if that makes any sense.
Are you still able to enjoy activities or hobbies that you usually find pleasurable?

Not really, no. I mean, it’s funny you ask that, because my wife was just pointing this out to me the other day. I used to have this whole routine, you know? Like, after a long night shift watching the cameras, I’d get home just as the sun was coming up, and I used to really look forward to my morning runs. I had this specific route that went down past the old middle school and around the park, and it was just... my way to clear my head, get some fresh air after being cooped up in the dark surveillance room all night. But lately, I just walk right past my running shoes. I look at them sitting there by the door, and the thought of actually putting them on and going outside just feels exhausting. I keep skipping the runs entirely because it just feels like this massive mountain to climb. 

And it’s not just the running, either. I have this old acoustic guitar, had it since high school, and I used to pick it up almost every afternoon when I woke up. Just strumming, maybe trying to learn a new song off the internet or just playing the same old chords, but it was nice. It was relaxing for me. Now, it’s just sitting on its stand in the corner of the living room, gathering dust. I’ll look at it, and instead of wanting to play, I just think about how much effort it takes to tune it and press down on the strings. I just can’t get myself to care about it anymore. 

Even cooking dinner... I used to be the one who’d cook for the family before I headed out for my shift. I’d actually enjoy it, you know, chopping the vegetables, getting everything going on the stove. It felt good to make something with my hands. But now, even that just feels like a chore. I keep skipping it and telling my wife to just order takeout or telling the kids to make sandwiches. Everything I used to actually like doing, it all just feels like a list of chores now that I can't get myself to care about. I just don't have the desire to do any of it.
Have you been having trouble sleeping lately?

Well, no, not really. I mean, my sleep schedule has always been a bit all over the place because of the night shifts, you know? Like I said, I work surveillance, so I'm usually clocking in around 10 PM and not getting out until 6 in the morning. So, sleeping during the day is just par for the course for me. I've got the blackout curtains in the bedroom, the white noise machine going to block out the neighborhood kids, the whole setup. 

But lately, honestly, if anything, I'm just sleeping more. I get home, I bypass the running shoes like I mentioned, and I just crash. And it's not even a restful sleep, if that makes sense. I’ll sleep for eight, maybe nine hours, and when my alarm goes off in the late afternoon, I just feel like I've been hit by a truck. I don't want to get out of bed. I’ll just lay there, staring at the ceiling, listening to my wife moving around in the kitchen, and the thought of actually getting up and starting my day just feels impossible. So, I don't know if you'd call that trouble sleeping, because I am sleeping, but it's just... I don't feel like I'm getting any energy from it. It’s just more time spent feeling heavy and flat, just horizontal instead of vertical.
Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?

Yeah, actually... it’s kind of weird you bring that up, because I probably wouldn't have really noticed it myself if it weren't for the guys at work. But they've definitely been saying something about it. 

We have these pre-shift briefings every night, right? Before we take over the monitor banks, the outgoing shift supervisor stands up at the front of that same break room I was telling you about earlier, and he goes over the rundown for the night. You know, going over the BOLO lists, any high-rollers on the casino floor we need to keep an extra eye on, any known card counters that security flagged earlier in the week. It’s usually a pretty fast-paced meeting because everyone just wants to get it over with and get to their stations. 

But lately... well, a couple of the guys have pointed out that I’m just moving a lot slower during those briefings. Like, my buddy Dave, who usually works the pit cameras, he actually nudged me the other night. The supervisor had asked me a direct question about a camera angle I’d been watching the night before, and I heard him, I knew exactly what he was asking, but it was like... I don't know, like my brain had to wade through molasses just to get the words down to my mouth. I just sat there for a good five seconds, staring at him, before I finally got the answer out. 

Dave pulled me aside after and asked if I was feeling okay, because he said I was taking way longer to answer people than I normally do. He even said that just watching me walk into the room and get my gear out of my locker, I looked sluggish. And when I really think about it, he's right. It just feels like my body and my mouth are both a full step behind everybody else. Like everyone else is moving and talking at normal speed, and I’m just stuck in slow motion trying to catch up to the conversation. It’s frustrating, especially in a job where you're supposed to be sharp and on the ball, but I just can't seem to force myself to move or talk any faster than this.
Do you often feel guilty about things?

Guilty? I don't... I don't think so. I mean, I feel bad that I'm not helping out around the house as much as I used to, like with the cooking and all that, but I wouldn't say I feel guilty about things in general. Like, I don't sit around beating myself up over things from the past or feeling like I've done something terrible. It's more just this overwhelming lack of energy and interest in everything. 

Like, my wife, she works days, right? She's a receptionist at a dental office downtown, so she's out the door by 7:30 every morning. And I know she's tired when she gets home, dealing with patients all day, answering phones, scheduling appointments. It's a lot. And I used to make sure dinner was ready or at least prepped before I left for my shift. Now, she comes home and has to figure it out, and I know that's not fair to her. I see her looking tired, trying to throw something together for the kids, and I just... I feel bad about it. But it's not this deep, crushing guilt that keeps me up at night. It's just a general feeling of, "Man, I wish I could get my act together and help out like I used to." 

But as for feeling guilty about other things, or feeling like a burden, or feeling like I've done something wrong... no, I don't really have that. I just feel kind of empty, you know? Like I'm just going through the motions, trying to get through each day, and I don't really have the energy to feel much of anything else, even guilt. It's just all so flat.
Have you been having any thoughts about hurting yourself?

No, no, definitely not. I mean, I don’t have any plans to do anything like that. I would never actually take steps to hurt myself, you know? I think about my wife, and the kids, and I know I couldn’t do that to them. They rely on me, even if I haven't been as helpful lately as I should be. So, no, no active plans or anything like that. 

But... well, I guess if I’m being completely honest, there is this thought that keeps creeping in lately. It usually happens right when I get home from my shift, around 6:30 or 7 in the morning. I’ll do my routine, you know, lock the front door, take off my boots in the hall so I don't wake anybody up, go into the bedroom, pull those heavy blackout curtains shut, and turn on the white noise machine. And then I just lay down. And in that quiet, before I actually drift off, I just feel this immense... weight. Like I was saying earlier, just heavy and flat. 

And lately, I keep having these thoughts where I catch myself thinking that maybe... maybe it wouldn't be the worst thing in the world if I just didn't wake up. Like, if I just went to sleep and that was it. It’s not that I want to die, really, it’s just that the idea of having to wake up at 4 PM, drag myself out of bed feeling like I got hit by a truck, try to force myself to make conversation with my wife, drive back to the casino, sit in that dark monitor room for another eight hours trying to force my brain to work... it just feels like so much effort. It’s like climbing a mountain every single day. And sometimes, lying there in the dark, I just think about how peaceful it would be to just stay asleep, to not have to keep pushing and pushing through all this everyday stuff that just feels so impossible right now. So, no, I'm not going to hurt myself, but... yeah, I guess I do think about just not waking up.
Do you often feel like you're worthless or a burden to others?

Worthless? A burden? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know I just mentioned feeling bad about not helping my wife with dinner and all that, but it doesn't cross over into feeling like I'm completely useless or dragging everyone down. I still go to work, you know? I still bring home a paycheck. 

I've been at the casino for almost twelve years now. Started out walking the floor, dealing with the drunks and the occasional dispute at the blackjack tables, and then worked my way up to the surveillance room. It's a steady job. The pay is decent, the benefits are good for the family. We've got full medical and dental, which is great since, like I said, my wife works at a dental office, but their insurance actually isn't as good as what the casino offers. Funny how that works out, right? Anyway, I know I'm providing for them. I know my income pays the mortgage on our house—it's a nice little three-bedroom ranch over in the new development on the west side of town. We just had the roof redone last summer, actually. Cost an arm and a leg, but it needed to be done. 

So, yeah, I know I contribute. I know I have a purpose in that sense. I don't sit around thinking I'm a waste of space or that they'd be better off without me financially or anything like that. It's just... I just don't have the drive I used to have. Like, I used to take the kids out on my days off, maybe go to the park or hit the batting cages. My oldest, he's ten, he's really getting into baseball now. Plays second base for his Little League team. Usually, I'd be out in the yard throwing grounders to him, trying to help him get his fielding down. But lately, on my days off, I just can't bring myself to get off the couch. I'll sit there watching TV, but not really watching it, you know? Just staring at the screen while the game is on, feeling completely drained. 

My wife will ask if I want to go to the store with her, or maybe take a drive up to the lake, and I just tell her I'm too tired. And I am tired. I'm exhausted all the time. But I don't feel like a burden to them because of it. They understand I work nights, they know it's a tough shift. I just feel like I'm not fully *there* for them right now. But worthless? No, I don't think I've ever used that word to describe how I feel. Just... empty. Just running on fumes.
Have you been feeling restless or fidgety lately?

Restless? No, not really. I don't get jittery or pace around or anything like that. Honestly, it's kind of the exact opposite lately. If anything, I just feel like I'm moving through molasses. 

It's actually gotten to the point where some of the guys at work have started making comments. We have these shift briefings, right? Every day before we take over the monitor room, the outgoing shift supervisor—usually this guy Stan, who’s been there forever, always drinks that terrible breakroom coffee—he gives us a rundown of what to watch out for. You know, like if there’s a known card counter on the floor, or if someone’s been loitering too long near the high-limit slots, or even just routine stuff like a pan-and-tilt camera being down for maintenance in the east corridor. It’s usually a pretty quick back-and-forth, rapid fire, getting the info so we can tag in and let the day shift go home. 

But lately... I don't know, people have noticed I'm just moving slower in those briefings. Stan asked me the other day if I was hungover, which I wasn't, I barely even drink. But he said I was taking way longer to answer when he’d ask me to confirm a camera zone or sign off on the handover sheet. It’s like... I hear what they’re saying, but it takes an extra second or two for my brain to process it and then send the signal to my mouth to actually speak. It's like my body and my mouth are both a step behind everybody else in the room. I’ll go to grab my logbook or reach for my radio, and my arm just feels heavy, like it takes a conscious effort to just lift it off the table. 

So, no, definitely not fidgety. Just... slow. Really, really slow. It’s frustrating, honestly, because I know the job inside and out. I've done it for over a decade. But I just can't seem to keep up with the normal pace of things right now, and I hate that the other guys are starting to pick up on it.
Have you lost interest in activities you once enjoyed?

Yeah, I really have. It’s funny you ask that, actually, because I was just looking at my guitar the other day and having that exact thought. 

I have this Fender Stratocaster, a really nice sunburst finish, that I bought second-hand back when I was in my twenties. I keep it down in the basement on a stand next to this little practice amp. Usually, on my nights off when the wife and kids are asleep, I’d go down there, plug in my headphones so I don't wake anybody up, and just noodle around for an hour or two. Mostly blues, some classic rock, that kind of stuff. It used to be my favorite way to unwind, you know? Just me and the strings, letting my brain decompress from the casino. But lately... it’s just sitting there gathering dust. I look at it, and instead of wanting to pick it up, it just feels like a chore. Like I’d have to tune it, and remember the chords, and make my fingers work, and I just... I can’t get myself to care enough to even take it off the stand. 

And it’s not just the guitar, either. I used to be pretty good about staying active. Working nights, you kind of have to be, or your body just falls apart on you. So I used to look forward to my morning runs right after I got off shift. I had this whole routine. Around 7:30 AM, before the neighborhood really got busy, I’d do this three-mile route down through the subdivision, past the elementary school, and loop back around the retention pond. I even bought these really nice, expensive Brooks running shoes last year specifically for it. But now? I get home, and the thought of lacing up those shoes and going back outside... it’s exhausting just thinking about it. I keep skipping them. Every morning I tell myself, "I'll go tomorrow," but tomorrow comes and I just walk right past the shoes, pull those blackout curtains shut, and lay down. It just feels like another heavy task on a to-do list that I don't want to look at.

Even stuff around the house, like... well, like I mentioned earlier about not helping my wife with dinner lately. I actually used to *love* cooking. It was kind of my thing. On my days off, I’d fire up the grill, or I’d make this really great chicken parmesan from scratch—like, actually breading the cutlets, simmering the sauce for a couple of hours. I used to really look forward to it. I'd plan the meals, go to the grocery store, pick out the ingredients. My wife loved it because it gave her a break after dealing with patients at the dental office all day. But now... the idea of standing in the kitchen, chopping onions, watching pots boil... I just can't do it. We've been ordering a lot of takeout, or she's been throwing frozen pizzas in the oven, because cooking just feels like this massive, insurmountable chore now. All these things I used to genuinely enjoy, they just feel like work now, and I just can't bring myself to care about doing them.
How many weeks have you been feeling this heavy, flat feeling?

Well, let me think... I'd say it's been right around three weeks now. It's actually pretty easy for me to pinpoint exactly when it started, because it was right around the time the suits at the casino decided to completely reorganize our security operations. 

You know how it is with corporate, right? Someone up top decides they need to justify their salary, so they come in and shake everything up even if it was working perfectly fine before. We had a really good system going in the surveillance room. I had my specific zones—mostly the high-limit blackjack tables, the baccarat room, and the main cashier's cage—and I knew the rhythm of it. I knew the dealers' tells, I knew the regulars, I knew exactly what to look for. 

But about three weeks ago, they rolled out this whole new operational matrix. They changed my assignments completely. Now they've got me rotating through the hotel corridors, the loading docks, and the parking garages, which is a completely different kind of monitoring. You're looking for car break-ins or people wandering the halls where they shouldn't be, instead of watching the actual games, which is what I'm actually good at. It's just a completely different vibe, and they didn't even really train us on the new protocols, they just handed us this massive binder at the start of the shift and said, "Here's your new rotation." 

I had to learn a whole new set of camera toggles and blind spots on the fly. And ever since that happened... yeah, about three weeks ago, that's when this whole heavy, flat feeling really settled in. Just right around the time they flipped my schedule and assignments upside down.
Would you say that you have lost interest in most things you used to enjoy, or is it more that you just don't feel like doing them right now?

Well... man, that’s a tough distinction, isn't it? But if I really sit down and think about it... it’s definitely that I’ve lost interest. It’s not just a temporary 'I'm too tired today' kind of thing. 

Like I was rambling about a minute ago with the guitar, and the morning runs, and cooking dinner for my wife... I used to genuinely look forward to those things. They were the highlights of my week, the stuff that kept me sane after staring at grainy security footage for eight hours. I used to have this app on my phone where I’d track my running pace down to the second, trying to beat my own time around that retention pond. And with the cooking, I’d obsess over getting the breading on the chicken just right, making sure the oil was the exact perfect temperature so it wouldn't get soggy. I cared about the details because I actually enjoyed the process. 

But lately, I just keep skipping all of it. And it’s not because I’m just putting it off until I have more energy—even if I try to tell myself that in the moment. It’s because they just feel like chores now. Massive, pointless chores that I absolutely cannot get myself to care about. I look at the Fender on the stand, or I look at those expensive running shoes, and there’s just... nothing. No spark, no itch to do it. It’s exactly the same feeling I get when I look at a pile of dirty laundry or a stack of bills. Just this heavy realization of 'ugh, I have to do this,' followed immediately by 'actually, I don't care, so I won't.' 

It’s a really weird place to be in, honestly, because I know I *should* care. I know these are the things that make up who I am outside of the casino. My wife even asked me about the cooking the other day, asking if we were ever going to do Italian night again, and I just had nothing to give her. That actual feeling of wanting to do any of it? It’s just completely evaporated. So yeah, I'd definitely say the interest itself is just gone.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past few weeks?

Weight? Well... I haven't exactly been stepping on the scale in the bathroom every morning to check, but I wouldn't be surprised if I dropped a few pounds, because my uniform belt is definitely sitting a notch looser lately. Actually, that's sort of a big part of why I came in to see you in the first place. For the last few weeks, I’ve just... I've barely had an appetite at all. 

Usually, working the overnight shift at the casino, you build up a pretty serious hunger by the time 6 AM rolls around. I used to have this whole routine where I'd hit up this 24-hour place on my way home. I'd get this massive Denver omelet or sometimes a double bacon cheeseburger—because when you work nights, breakfast is basically your dinner, right? You need something heavy in your stomach so you can sleep through the day. But lately... I don't even bother stopping. 

And if I do bring something home, or if my wife leaves some leftovers out in the fridge for me, it just... it just sits there on the counter. Even foods I usually really like, stuff I’d normally look forward to tearing into after a long shift of staring at those monitors, I just end up staring at the plate. I'll sit there at the kitchen island, the house is all quiet, and I literally have to force down a few bites just so I don't wake up with stomach cramps later. After three or four bites, it just feels like I'm chewing on cardboard, and I end up wrapping the rest in foil and shoving it back in the fridge. It’s like my brain just completely forgot how to be hungry. So, yeah, if I have lost a significant amount of weight, it's definitely because I'm basically just running on empty most days.
Have you been experiencing any significant changes in your energy levels throughout the day?

Energy levels? Man, that's... well, I haven't really noticed any big changes there, to be honest. I mean, working the graveyard shift, your energy is always a little weird anyway, right? You're essentially fighting thousands of years of human evolution that says you should be asleep when it's dark outside. So you get used to this sort of baseline fatigue, this low-level hum of exhaustion that just lives in your bones. 

Like, around 3 or 4 AM, there's always that dip. We call it 'hitting the wall' in the surveillance room. The casino floor is usually dead quiet by then—unless it's a holiday weekend or there's a big convention in town—and you're just staring at these screens showing empty hallways and bored dealers. Your eyes start to cross, and you have to get up, stretch your legs, maybe grab a cup of that terrible breakroom coffee that tastes like burnt copper, just to keep yourself focused. That's always been there. 

But as far as my energy levels changing recently? Along with everything else that's been going on over the last three weeks? I can't really say that I've noticed a difference. I'm not suddenly crashing in the middle of my shift or feeling like I have to sleep for fourteen hours straight when I get home. I still get off work, drive home, and try to wind down. I still have enough physical energy to do things, you know? Like, I *could* go for a run or I *could* pick up the guitar. My arms and legs work fine. I'm not physically wiped out. 

It's more just... what I was saying earlier. The desire is gone. The physical energy is there, exactly the same as it always was, but the mental energy, the spark to actually use it? That's what's missing. So, no, physically, my energy levels feel pretty much the same as they always have. Just the standard night shift grogginess, nothing new or significant on that front.
Have you been feeling like you're moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or have others commented on this?

Moving slower? Yeah, actually... it's funny you bring that up, because I wouldn't have necessarily put it together myself if it wasn't for the guys at work saying something. 

It’s weird because, like I was just saying about my energy levels, I don't feel physically exhausted in a way where my muscles are giving out, but there is definitely this... this lag. You see, before every single shift, we have this pass-down briefing. The swing shift guys are clocking out, usually eager to hit the bars or just go home to bed, and us graveyard guys are just coming in. The shift supervisor stands at the front of the room and rattles off all the active stuff—known card counters who got spotted, suspected cheats, VIPs who need extra camera monitoring, any machines that are down, that kind of thing. It's a very rapid-fire environment because the outgoing shift just wants to leave. 

But lately, I’m just... I don't know, it's like I'm wading through molasses. Dave, our supervisor, will ask me a direct question, like, 'Hey, did you finish reviewing the tape on table 44 from yesterday?' and I'll just sit there. It takes me a second to even register that he said my name, and then another couple of seconds to actually formulate the words to reply. I'm just taking way longer to answer than I normally would. 

A couple of the guys have definitely noticed. My buddy Mike actually nudged me during Tuesday's briefing and asked if I was hungover—which I wasn't, I don't drink before a shift—but he said I was just moving in slow motion. Getting my gear together, clipping on my radio, grabbing my logs... even just walking from the briefing room down the hall to the surveillance pit, I'm just dragging. People are literally walking past me in the hall. 

It really feels exactly like my body and my mouth are both just a step behind everybody else. Being a surveillance guy, the best way I can describe it is like when the audio and video are out of sync on a bad camera feed, you know? The rest of the room is playing at normal speed, and I'm just stuck on a delayed feed, trying to catch up to the conversation but I just can't seem to force myself to talk or move any faster. So, yeah, people have definitely been pointing it out.
Have you noticed any significant change in your weight recently?

Wait, didn't we... I think I mentioned this right when we first sat down, didn't I? About my uniform belt fitting looser and all that? But, yeah, to reiterate... that's honestly the main reason I finally decided to come in and make this appointment in the first place. 

For the last few weeks, I’ve just barely had an appetite at all. It's completely vanished. Like I was saying earlier, I'll get off my shift, and even if it's foods I usually really like—stuff I'd normally crave after ten hours of staring at monitors in the surveillance pit—it just sits there on the plate. My wife made my absolute favorite baked ziti the other day, left a huge portion in the fridge for me, and I just sat at the kitchen island staring at it while it got cold. I literally had to force down a few bites just to have something in my system, and even that felt like a massive chore. I'm just eating way, way less than I used to, so if my weight is dropping, that's exactly why. It's just so strange, you know? Looking at a meal you normally love and just feeling absolutely nothing.
Have you been having any thoughts about hurting yourself that you've thought about acting on?

Hurting myself? Like... actually doing something to myself? No, no, I'm not planning anything like that. I don't have a plan, I haven't been looking up ways to do it or anything like that. I'm not sitting in the surveillance room eyeing the rafters or whatever. 

But... I mean, I'm not going to lie to you, my mind has been going to some pretty dark places lately. It's not about actively wanting to end it, it's more just this... this overwhelming exhaustion with everything. Like I said about the energy, the physical energy is there, but the mental part is just shot. So when I get home after a shift, and the house is quiet, and I'm just sitting there in the dark because my wife is still asleep... I start thinking. And lately, those thoughts have been, well, they've been kind of heavy. 

I keep catching myself thinking that maybe... maybe it just wouldn't be the worst thing in the world if I went to sleep and just didn't wake up. You know? Not that I want to kill myself, but just... if it happened naturally, if my heart just stopped or something, it would mean I wouldn't have to keep doing this. I wouldn't have to keep waking up and putting on the uniform and going into the pit and staring at the monitors and feeling like I'm moving through wet concrete and forcing down food I don't want. It's just so much effort to just exist right now. 

It's like... imagine you're watching a movie, right? And it's just dragging on, and the plot is terrible, and you're not enjoying it at all. You don't necessarily want to smash the TV, but if the power went out and the screen just went black, you wouldn't exactly be upset about it. You'd probably just be relieved that you didn't have to sit through the rest of it. That's kind of where my head is at. It's just this constant, passive thought of, 'Man, it would be so much easier if I just didn't have to push through this anymore.' But as far as actually taking steps to make that happen? No, I haven't thought about acting on it. I wouldn't do that to my wife. But the thoughts... yeah, they're definitely there, just sort of humming in the background.
Would you say your feelings of heaviness and flatness are present every day?

Every day? Well... I don't know if I'd say every single day without fail, but definitely most days. Yeah, most days for sure. It's just this... this heavy, flat feeling that I'm carrying around with me, and it doesn't seem to matter where I am or what's going on around me. 

Like, I could be sitting in the break room at work—we've got this little room right off the surveillance pit with a couple of beat-up couches and a TV that's pretty much permanently glued to SportsCenter. The other guys will be in there on their meal breaks, eating, joking around, maybe laughing about some guy who got himself eighty-sixed from the blackjack tables earlier that night. Just normal break room stuff, right? And I'll be sitting right there on the couch next to them, but I'm just... I'm not really there. It's like I'm totally disconnected from the room, just completely flat while everyone else is carrying on normally. 

And it's the exact same thing at home, too. That's the part that really bothers me. Even when I'm off shift and I'm just sitting in the living room with my wife, trying to watch a show or just, you know, be present with my family... that heaviness is still right there sitting on my chest. I'm physically in the room with her, but mentally I'm just totally checked out. It's like there's this invisible wall between me and everything else. So, yeah, I'd say most days it's just this constant weight I'm dragging around, no matter if I'm at the casino or in my own house.

It’s exactly the same feeling I get when I look at a pile of dirty laundry or a stack of bills. Just this heavy realization of 'ugh, I have to do this,' followed immediately by 'actually, I don't care, so I won't.' 

It’s a really weird place to be in, honestly, because I know I *should* care. I know these are the things that make up who I am outside of the casino. My wife even asked me about the cooking the other day, asking if we were ever going to do Italian night again, and I just had nothing to give her. That actual feeling of wanting to do any of it? It’s just completely evaporated. So yeah, I'd definitely say the interest itself is just gone.

target_item.manifestation: I came in because for the last few weeks I’ve barely had an appetite, and even foods I usually like after a shift just sit there while I force down a few bites.

patient.answer:
Weight? Well... I haven't exactly been stepping on the scale in the bathroom every morning to check, but I wouldn't be surprised if I dropped a few pounds, because my uniform belt is definitely sitting a notch looser lately. Actually, that's sort of a big part of why I came in to see you in the first place. For the last few weeks, I’ve just... I've barely had an appetite at all. 

Usually, working the overnight shift at the casino, you build up a pretty serious hunger by the time 6 AM rolls around. I used to have this whole routine where I'd hit up this 24-hour place on my way home. I'd get this massive Denver omelet or sometimes a double bacon cheeseburger—because when you work nights, breakfast is basically your dinner, right? You need something heavy in your stomach so you can sleep through the day. But lately... I don't even bother stopping. 

And if I do bring something home, or if my wife leaves some leftovers out in the fridge for me, it just... it just sits there on the counter. Even foods I usually really like, stuff I’d normally look forward to tearing into after a long shift of staring at those monitors, I just end up staring at the plate. I'll sit there at the kitchen island, the house is all quiet, and I literally have to force down a few bites just so I don't wake up with stomach cramps later. After three or four bites, it just feels like I'm chewing on cardboard, and I end up wrapping the rest in foil and shoving it back in the fridge. It’s like my brain just completely forgot how to be hungry. So, yeah, if I have lost a significant amount of weight, it's definitely because I'm basically just running on empty most days.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive symptoms
doctor.question: Have you been experiencing any significant changes in your energy levels throughout the day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in energy levels (fatigue/loss of energy), which corresponds to S027. This symptom is not present in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Energy levels? Man, that's... well, I haven't really noticed any big changes there, to be honest. I mean, working the graveyard shift, your energy is always a little weird anyway, right? You're essentially fighting thousands of years of human evolution that says you should be asleep when it's dark outside. So you get used to this sort of baseline fatigue, this low-level hum of exhaustion that just lives in your bones. 

Like, around 3 or 4 AM, there's always that dip. We call it 'hitting the wall' in the surveillance room. The casino floor is usually dead quiet by then—unless it's a holiday weekend or there's a big convention in town—and you're just staring at these screens showing empty hallways and bored dealers. Your eyes start to cross, and you have to get up, stretch your legs, maybe grab a cup of that terrible breakroom coffee that tastes like burnt copper, just to keep yourself focused. That's always been there. 

But as far as my energy levels changing recently? Along with everything else that's been going on over the last three weeks? I can't really say that I've noticed a difference. I'm not suddenly crashing in the middle of my shift or feeling like I have to sleep for fourteen hours straight when I get home. I still get off work, drive home, and try to wind down. I still have enough physical energy to do things, you know? Like, I *could* go for a run or I *could* pick up the guitar. My arms and legs work fine. I'm not physically wiped out. 

It's more just... what I was saying earlier. The desire is gone. The physical energy is there, exactly the same as it always was, but the mental energy, the spark to actually use it? That's what's missing. So, no, physically, my energy levels feel pretty much the same as they always have. Just the standard night shift grogginess, nothing new or significant on that front.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation to differentiate between F32.0, F32.1, F32.2, and F32.3
doctor.question: Have you been feeling like you're moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or have others commented on this?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: At work people have noticed I’m moving slower in briefings and taking longer to answer, like my body and my mouth are both a step behind everybody else.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about moving or speaking more slowly and if others have noticed, which directly maps to psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Moving slower? Yeah, actually... it's funny you bring that up, because I wouldn't have necessarily put it together myself if it wasn't for the guys at work saying something. 

It’s weird because, like I was just saying about my energy levels, I don't feel physically exhausted in a way where my muscles are giving out, but there is definitely this... this lag. You see, before every single shift, we have this pass-down briefing. The swing shift guys are clocking out, usually eager to hit the bars or just go home to bed, and us graveyard guys are just coming in. The shift supervisor stands at the front of the room and rattles off all the active stuff—known card counters who got spotted, suspected cheats, VIPs who need extra camera monitoring, any machines that are down, that kind of thing. It's a very rapid-fire environment because the outgoing shift just wants to leave. 

But lately, I’m just... I don't know, it's like I'm wading through molasses. Dave, our supervisor, will ask me a direct question, like, 'Hey, did you finish reviewing the tape on table 44 from yesterday?' and I'll just sit there. It takes me a second to even register that he said my name, and then another couple of seconds to actually formulate the words to reply. I'm just taking way longer to answer than I normally would. 

A couple of the guys have definitely noticed. My buddy Mike actually nudged me during Tuesday's briefing and asked if I was hungover—which I wasn't, I don't drink before a shift—but he said I was just moving in slow motion. Getting my gear together, clipping on my radio, grabbing my logs... even just walking from the briefing room down the hall to the surveillance pit, I'm just dragging. People are literally walking past me in the hall. 

It really feels exactly like my body and my mouth are both just a step behind everybody else. Being a surveillance guy, the best way I can describe it is like when the audio and video are out of sync on a bad camera feed, you know? The rest of the room is playing at normal speed, and I'm just stuck on a delayed feed, trying to catch up to the conversation but I just can't seem to force myself to talk or move any faster. So, yeah, people have definitely been pointing it out.

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I’m not planning to hurt myself, but I keep having these thoughts that maybe it wouldn’t be the worst thing if I didn’t wake up and didn’t have to keep pushing through all this.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thoughts of self-harm or suicide, which directly corresponds to the Death_Suicide symptom.

patient.answer:
Hurting myself? Like... actually doing something to myself? No, no, I'm not planning anything like that. I don't have a plan, I haven't been looking up ways to do it or anything like that. I'm not sitting in the surveillance room eyeing the rafters or whatever. 

But... I mean, I'm not going to lie to you, my mind has been going to some pretty dark places lately. It's not about actively wanting to end it, it's more just this... this overwhelming exhaustion with everything. Like I said about the energy, the physical energy is there, but the mental part is just shot. So when I get home after a shift, and the house is quiet, and I'm just sitting there in the dark because my wife is still asleep... I start thinking. And lately, those thoughts have been, well, they've been kind of heavy. 

I keep catching myself thinking that maybe... maybe it just wouldn't be the worst thing in the world if I went to sleep and just didn't wake up. You know? Not that I want to kill myself, but just... if it happened naturally, if my heart just stopped or something, it would mean I wouldn't have to keep doing this. I wouldn't have to keep waking up and putting on the uniform and going into the pit and staring at the monitors and feeling like I'm moving through wet concrete and forcing down food I don't want. It's just so much effort to just exist right now. 

It's like... imagine you're watching a movie, right? And it's just dragging on, and the plot is terrible, and you're not enjoying it at all. You don't necessarily want to smash the TV, but if the power went out and the screen just went black, you wouldn't exactly be upset about it. You'd probably just be relieved that you didn't have to sit through the rest of it. That's kind of where my head is at. It's just this constant, passive thought of, 'Man, it would be so much easier if I just didn't have to push through this anymore.' But as far as actually taking steps to make that happen? No, I haven't thought about acting on it. I wouldn't do that to my wife. But the thoughts... yeah, they're definitely there, just sort of humming in the background.

patient.answer:
Every day? Well... I don't know if I'd say every single day without fail, but definitely most days. Yeah, most days for sure. It's just this... this heavy, flat feeling that I'm carrying around with me, and it doesn't seem to matter where I am or what's going on around me. 

Like, I could be sitting in the break room at work—we've got this little room right off the surveillance pit with a couple of beat-up couches and a TV that's pretty much permanently glued to SportsCenter. The other guys will be in there on their meal breaks, eating, joking around, maybe laughing about some guy who got himself eighty-sixed from the blackjack tables earlier that night. Just normal break room stuff, right? And I'll be sitting right there on the couch next to them, but I'm just... I'm not really there. It's like I'm totally disconnected from the room, just completely flat while everyone else is carrying on normally. 

And it's the exact same thing at home, too. That's the part that really bothers me. Even when I'm off shift and I'm just sitting in the living room with my wife, trying to watch a show or just, you know, be present with my family... that heaviness is still right there sitting on my chest. I'm physically in the room with her, but mentally I'm just totally checked out. It's like there's this invisible wall between me and everything else. So, yeah, I'd say most days it's just this constant weight I'm dragging around, no matter if I'm at the casino or in my own house.

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the patient's loss of interest in activities
doctor.question: How long have you felt like you've lost interest in the things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to look forward to my morning runs, playing guitar, and cooking dinner, but lately I keep skipping them because they just feel like chores I can’t get myself to care about.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about the duration of my loss of interest in things I used to enjoy, which maps perfectly to the Loss_of_Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
How long? Um, let me think. It's been... well, it's been a gradual thing, I guess, but I'd say it's been going on for a few weeks now. At least a few weeks where it's been really noticeable to me. 

See, I used to have this whole routine. I've always been a pretty active guy, you know? Being in the surveillance room all day, you get stiff, so I used to really look forward to my morning runs. I'd get up early, lace up my sneakers, hit the pavement before the neighborhood even woke up. It was my time to just clear my head, get the blood pumping. And then, in the evenings, I'd pick up my guitar. I'm no Eric Clapton or anything, but I've been playing since high school. Just strumming some chords, learning a new song... it was relaxing. And cooking, too. I mentioned my wife making the baked ziti earlier, but honestly, I used to be the one making dinner half the time. I liked finding new recipes, chopping vegetables, just the whole process of putting a meal together. 

But lately... man, for the last few weeks, I just keep skipping all of it. Every single bit of it. I'll wake up and look at my running shoes by the door, and I just... I can't. I just think about how heavy my legs are going to feel, and how much effort it's going to take, and I just turn over and go back to sleep. And the guitar? It's just sitting there on the stand in the corner of the living room, gathering dust. I look at it and I don't feel any desire to pick it up. It's like... it's like the part of my brain that used to get enjoyment out of those things just got switched off. 

Even the cooking. Now, the thought of standing in the kitchen, prepping ingredients, standing over a hot stove... it just feels like this massive chore. It's not fun anymore. None of it is fun. It all just feels like work that I can't get myself to care about. So I just don't do them. I come home, I sit down, and I do nothing. It's been like this for weeks, and it's just... it's really frustrating, because I know I used to love doing these things, and now I just couldn't care less.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of guilt or worthlessness
doctor.question: Do you feel guilty or worthless about not being able to do the things you used to enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt or worthlessness, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Worthless? Um... no. No, I wouldn't say that. 

I mean, I know it probably sounds like I should, right? You hear about guys who stop pulling their weight or stop doing the things they're supposed to do, and they sit around feeling like a piece of garbage about it. But honestly? I don't really feel bad about it. It's not a pity party I'm throwing for myself. 

It's more just... apathy, I guess? Like, to feel guilty, you have to actually care that you're not doing the thing. You have to feel like you're letting yourself down or letting someone else down. And that's the whole problem right now—I just don't care enough to feel bad about it. 

Take the cooking, for example. Used to be, if I planned to make dinner and then just totally bailed on it, I'd feel terrible. I'd be apologizing to my wife up and down, maybe offering to order takeout from that Italian place down the street to make up for it, feeling like a jerk for leaving her hanging. But now, when I just sit on the couch instead of going into the kitchen, I don't feel bad. I don't sit there thinking, 'Man, I'm a worthless husband, I can't even boil water.' I just sit there. She ends up making something or we just eat cereal, and I don't even flinch.

Same with the running. Years ago, if I skipped a morning run, I'd be kicking myself all day. I'd be up in the surveillance pit, pacing behind the monitors, feeling all antsy and annoyed with myself for being lazy. I'd be mentally calculating how many extra miles I'd have to do the next day to make up for it. Now? I look at the shoes, I decide not to run, and that's the absolute end of the thought process. There's no inner critic beating me up over it. 

It's almost like... like the part of my brain that would normally make me feel guilty is just as tired as the rest of me. It takes energy to feel worthless, you know? You have to actively put yourself down and dwell on it. And I just don't have the juice for that. It's just a blank. So, no, no guilt or anything like that. Just... nothing.
